comparator.name: Earth System Sciences
comparator.sourceNotes: The current BSW2026 handbook defines 117 EC compulsory credited courses, 3 EC preparation-dependent mathematics/statistics, 18 EC advanced restricted options, 12 EC thesis and 30 EC genuine minor/electives =180. The illustrated Mathematics A preparation requires MAT14803; Mathematics B students take Statistics1 instead. This is not an arbitrary official-order mathematics choice. The generic target has no named academic track: choose the first three advanced options in current official order, Hydrogeology, Python and SedimentaryGeology, with their preceding common courses and practical-safety conditions. The old2025scheme is historical orientation, not the controlling curriculum. Thesis entry requires102mandatory/restricted credits including all60B1 plus the first two years of personal-development assignments (or coordinator-agreed subset); supervisor topic assumptions remain distinct from hard credits. The12ECindividual research includes proposal, field/lab/modelling or existing-data analysis, report, symposium, oral discussion and ethics. Topic allocation follows two annual cycles and the stated6month completion rule applies when delay is not planned/force-majeure. Noncredit practical safety and the three-year personal-development path are not added to180EC. Public programme and current handbook confirm English instruction and scientific soil/water/atmosphere/biosphere identity.
components: The programme also includes non-credit personal development across three years. General, laboratory and fieldwork safety training applies to the relevant practical activities; these requirements are not extra EC.

WUR studies atmospheric thermodynamics, radiation, cloud physics, chemistry and dynamics quantitatively. UCR’s Climate Change course addresses greenhouse forcing, feedbacks and impacts, without the same dedicated atmospheric-physics sequence.
This example uses Mathematics Applied: Introduction for students with VWO Mathematics A. Students with Mathematics B take Statistics 1 instead; the choice follows prior preparation and study advice.
System Earth: Climate and Global Change
Chemical Processes in Soil, Water, Atmosphere

WUR explicitly models soil–vegetation–atmosphere exchanges, evapotranspiration, radiation and transport. General ecological energy and matter cycles at UCR do not reproduce that coupled physical sequence.
Geology, Soils and Landscapes of the Northwest European Lowlands

One of three selected advanced options. This course combines aquifer systems, groundwater modelling and field investigation. It assumes earlier water-analysis and water-quantity/quality study and requires fieldwork safety.
One of three selected advanced options. This course develops Python programming for scientific data work; it assumes elementary computer skills.
Sedimentary Geology of Lowlands: Principles, Methods and Applications

One of three selected advanced options. This course studies sedimentary successions and lowland stratigraphy through field and laboratory methods. It builds on the common geology course and requires laboratory and fieldwork safety.
The illustrated pathway preserves 30 EC for a minor and/or individually chosen electives. Optional data-science courses or a named minor are not made compulsory.

The required 12 EC thesis is individual Earth-system research. Entry requires at least 102 EC of compulsory and restricted courses, all 60 first-year EC, and the first two years of personal-development assignments or an agreed subset. Supervisors may specify prior-course knowledge for a topic. UCR’s optional 15 EC independent research is additional to the illustrated 180 EC.

core: Earth-system interactions among soil, water, atmosphere and the biosphere
Physics, chemistry, mathematics, statistics, modelling and field measurement
Climate, weather and global environmental change
adjacent: Soils, geology, landscapes and sustainable land use
Hydrology, groundwater, water quality and river systems
Atmospheric processes, meteorology and climate dynamics
Geo-information, environmental data and computational modelling
Flood, drought, hazards, adaptation and disaster resilience
Ecology and biosphere interactions within Earth systems
questions: How can soil and water systems be understood and managed under floods, drought and land-use change?
How do atmospheric and climate processes interact with ecosystems and landscapes?
How can field measurement, spatial evidence and models reveal changes across the Earth system?

alternatives.label: Earth systems, climate & environmental evidence
alternatives.labelReason: Study geological, soil, water and climate processes through field and laboratory evidence, geochemical and numerical models, ecological relationships and environmental responses. Energy systems and governance connect that scientific understanding to practical sustainability questions.
alternatives.concept: Study geological, soil, water and climate processes through field and laboratory evidence, geochemical and numerical models, ecological relationships and environmental responses. Energy systems and governance connect that scientific understanding to practical sustainability questions.
progression: Current fixed-term X offerings and all formal prerequisites checked. Sustainability Essentials I precedes II and Earth System Science Tools; calculus precedes probability, linear algebra/numerical methods and deep learning; Python precedes algorithms. Dynamic Earth moves to its first planned Fall2027 offering; earlier Earth-system tools have a completed sustainability foundation and no geology prerequisite. The ecology option places molecular/cellular foundations before evolution and marine ecology. No additional advisory hard constraints are invented.

alternatives.labelReason: Study how soil and water processes interact with biodiversity, ecosystems and land use. Combine geoscience and environmental chemistry with ecological measurement, conservation, farming, nature-based water management and environmental justice.

trace: Chemical/thermodynamic/mechanical principles, nutrient and carbon boundaries, elementary differential models and laboratory measurement provide direct foundations for Earth-system processes. Its biopolymer experiment is a material-science practical, not hydrological field measurement.

Organismal/phylogenetic diversity, ecological roles, biodiversity indices, identification and data collection/analysis give concrete biosphere knowledge and measurement for Earth-system and ecosystem questions.

Python control flow, collections, functions, recursion, object-oriented construction and testing/debugging supply concrete scientific-computing foundations. Environmental datasets are possible applications, not guaranteed gateway content.

Actual wave physics, optical spectroscopy, chemical analysis, microscopic materials and stress/strain supply physical and chemical methods for geoscience and environmental evidence. The final greenwashing communication project is not integrated Earth-system modelling.

Calculus, optimisation, differential equations, dynamic-model implementation and numerical approximation supply actual quantitative tools for environmental process models. The selected detailed evidence is not a separate linear-algebra sequence.

The available description substantively supports geoscience risk analysis, climate-related/mining disasters, drought and toxic-algal hazards and adaptation. It supplies direct environmental-risk content without invented modelling software or field assessment methods.

The description directly supports biosphere/hydrosphere/lithosphere/atmosphere interactions, system modelling, proxies/isotope tracers and past/future climate, with a greenhouse-gas-pathways field trip. These receive full consideration; particular tracer protocols or software are not inferred.

Greenhouse gases, feedbacks/tipping points, sea-level/ocean/ecological impacts and mitigation/adaptation provide substantive climate-system knowledge. Stakeholder interviews and a climate film do not constitute quantitative atmospheric-dynamics training.

Rocks/minerals, sedimentation/facies, structural deformation, stratigraphy and tectonic/geophysical processes directly implement geological Earth science, including field mapping, cross-sections and reconstruction of geological history.
R data cleaning, joins, exploration/visualisation and actual spatial-data workflows provide direct methods for environmental evidence. It does not guarantee a climate or water project.

Probability, multivariate distributions, estimation/testing, Bayesian updating and Monte Carlo/Gibbs sampling supply concrete uncertainty and inference methods for observations and models. Applications and software differ from WUR’s introductory applied statistics.

ArcGIS spatial-data models, projections, queries/transformations, surface analysis and remote-sensing acquisition/image processing directly implement geospatial environmental inquiry and a collaborative environmental case study.

Soil formation/properties/chemistry/biology, shallow aquifers, salinization and seismic/resistivity/electromagnetic surveys directly support soil and subsurface-water investigation. Field/lab measurement is substantial; a full groundwater-flow model sequence is not promised.

Actual delta flooding, freshwater scarcity, salinization, subsidence, pollution and engineered/nature-based responses supply concrete water-management and adaptation study. Site-based Zeeland inquiry differs from dedicated catchment-flow equations and water/atmosphere balance measurement.

Numerical root finding, integration, ODE and linear/nonlinear-system solvers, error, stability and convergence supply concrete scientific-modelling tools. Broad multivariate PDE/vector-calculus coverage is not inferred.

Aqueous speciation, carbonate/redox/mineral/surface chemistry, weathering and biological controls directly implement environmental biogeochemistry. Laboratory evidence and geochemical equilibrium/speciation models support contamination, remediation and resource questions.

Solar/wind/hydro/geothermal/biomass physics, yield calculations, energy storage and system reliability connect climate-response choices to actual resource constraints. Polysun and mini-grid analyses are energy-system applications, not atmospheric circulation models.

Actual phytoremediation/mycoremediation, soil amendments, chemical leaching and metal-recovery laboratory work support contamination intervention and resource circularity. E-waste/panel recycling is a complementary materials theme; it is not the whole of soil science.

Regression/classification, resampling, regularisation, trees, dimension reduction and held-out prediction evaluation supply real environmental-data modelling tools. Particular geospatial or climate applications are not guaranteed.

The description supports substantial geoscientific research on nuclear-waste storage, geothermal energy and CO2 capture through literature review, reports and professional presentation. This is direct subsurface/resource inquiry, not documented lowland sedimentary logging or a required bachelor thesis.

Food/water/energy/climate governance, institutions, power, stakeholders and policy-option appraisal provide specific tools for assessing responses to environmental change. The Zeeland policy project does not substitute for hydrological or geological science.

The description supports technical/economic energy-use assessment, solar/wind/bioenergy choices and a partner report/presentation. This directly applies climate-mitigation questions; it does not supply a meteorological or individual thesis equivalent.

Environmental conditions/resources, ecological population/community dynamics, food webs and ecosystem energy/matter fluxes, including R ecological models and a research project, directly implement the biosphere side of Earth-system interactions. Coupled canopy evapotranspiration/soil transport is not established.

Nature-based infrastructure, coastal/river/estuary management, habitat connectivity and intervention design supply a concrete adaptation application linking physical water risks to ecosystem processes.

Vectors/matrices, eigenvalues, projections, least squares, SVD/PCA and dynamical/Markov applications provide substantial linear-algebra tools for spatial datasets, multivariate models and image/predictive methods.

Data structures, sorting/searching/graph algorithms, performance analysis and experimental benchmarking support reliable computational handling of spatial/network data and modelling workloads. No Earth-specific algorithm or satellite project is guaranteed.

Python/Keras/TensorFlow neural models, regularisation, time-series/image learning and predictive experimentation extend environmental-data methods. Independent image/text project choices are real; a climate forecast or Earth-science dataset is not guaranteed.

Python/OpenCV spatial/spectral image representations, filtering, segmentation, feature tracking and recognition-pipeline benchmarking substantively support image-based environmental observation. Earth Observation supplies the actual geospatial domain; this course does not promise satellite imagery.

Biomolecules, cells, enzymes/energy metabolism, DNA/heredity and gene expression supply concrete molecular foundations for the ecological option’s evolution, microbial/biogeochemical and biodiversity study. Biomedical examples are complementary; human disease is not presented as an Earth-system specialism.

Habitat loss/fragmentation, climate impacts, invasive species, conservation priorities and threatened-species assessment provide concrete ecosystem-resilience responses to environmental and land-use pressures.

Selection, genetic drift, adaptation, population genetics, phylogeny and biogeography supply specific biological mechanisms for changing communities and biodiversity. They complement ecosystem response and do not substitute for soil/water physics.

Physical/chemical oceanography, primary/secondary production, microbial and estuarine/marine ecosystems, acidification and human impacts support coastal biosphere–water interactions. Marine outreach methods do not establish hydrological instrumentation.

Environmental impacts of agriculture, biodiversity/ecosystem effects and comparative appraisal of alternative farming practices directly support land-use, soil/water and biosphere resilience. Its literature project is not a prescribed soil-physics field experiment.

The description supports actual environmental-justice and social-movement cases, including anti-colonial/feminist/degrowth perspectives. These provide a specific societal appraisal of environmental interventions and affected communities; not a physical hazard model.
blocks: Shared Python structured programming, collections, functions and scientific data handling. Specific libraries and application projects differ.

Shared calculus, differentiation/integration and first-order differential equations. UCR additionally implements dynamic models and numerical tools; the preparation-dependent introductory choice remains separate.
Shared vector/matrix algebra, linear systems, eigenvalues, projections/regression and mathematical software. UCR also develops vector spaces, SVD and PCA.

Shared numerical ODE/system solution, integration, error and stability analysis. WUR additionally develops multivariable integration, PDEs and vector-field transport; this is partial methods correspondence.
Shared probability, estimation and statistical inference. UCR is broader mathematical probability with simulation/Bayesian elements; WUR supplies introductory applied inference.
No selected dedicated introductory general-chemistry course. Environmental chemistry within sustainability/biogeochemistry does not reproduce the complete requirement.
Sustainability foundations include mechanics/waves/thermodynamics, but no selected standalone introductory-physics sequence is equated to this course.
No separate second general-chemistry unit is selected.
The preparation-dependent introductory mathematics/statistics option remains separate; UCR Mathematical Methods is aligned once to the substantive applied-analysis course.

Both use geological/Earth-system observation and field inquiry. UCR focuses on geology, rocks, tectonics and geological history; WUR’s introduction integrates soil, water and atmosphere through three interdisciplinary field cases.

Shared Earth-system interactions, climate change and system modelling, with geochemical/tracer evidence at UCR. WUR integrates hydrology, meteorology and biogeochemistry through an intensive modelling activity.

Shared greenhouse forcing, climate feedbacks and environmental consequences. WUR has a broader quantitative thermodynamics/cloud/radiation/dynamics/air-quality foundation; UCR does not reproduce that specialist physical sequence.
Shared aqueous speciation, mineral-water/sediment/surface chemistry and quantitative geochemical interpretation. WUR additionally treats atmospheric and cloud chemistry.
No selected course guarantees the coordinated nine-credit field/lab/computer Earth-system budget and land-use integration project.
No dedicated quantitative meteorology sequence is selected.
Dynamic Earth supplies geological methods, but does not reproduce the region-specific integration of northwest-European geology, soils and landscapes.

Earth’s Resources supports subsurface resource/storage research but its available description does not establish sedimentary-successions logging, stratigraphy and lowland field/lab methods. Dynamic Earth already has its strongest adequate placement.

Shared aquifer properties, groundwater/salinization investigation and field evidence. WUR further develops regional groundwater-flow models and hydrochemical/isotope applications; UCR emphasises soils and applied geophysical surveys.

Shared freshwater availability, water quality, salinization, flooding and water-management responses. WUR adds detailed catchment equations and chemical/biological field/lab measurement; UCR integrates governance and adaptation.

Shared contaminant behaviour and soil remediation, including actual phytoremediation/mycoremediation and chemical laboratory work at UCR. WUR additionally treats nutrient dynamics, soil-biota relations, standards and wider soil-quality assessment.

Shared ecological conditions/resources, populations, communities, ecosystems, biodiversity and human impacts. UCR additionally uses R ecological models; WUR supplies its own introductory practical context.
Water topics are distributed across UCR courses; no additional canonical course is assigned to reproduce this introductory exploratory unit.
UCR soils and geology provide related content; no separate soil-geography course is selected.
The strongest water counterpart is aligned once to Water Quantity and Quality; this distinct first-year analytical component retains a gap.
Soil formation and chemistry appear at UCR, but no second canonical row is forced to reproduce this distinct introductory soil-processes course.
General ecological energy/matter fluxes are not dedicated coupled soil–vegetation–atmosphere evapotranspiration, radiation and vadose-zone transport modelling.

Shared practical data handling, analysis and interpretation as an identifiable environmental-research skill. WUR combines introductory data work with information literacy, group collaboration and a programme-specific broad case; UCR concentrates on R data workflows.
Shared geospatial data models, reference/projections, queries/transformations, terrain/surface analysis, remote-sensing foundations and image processing with professional GIS software.
No selected course guarantees WUR’s coordinated catchment-scale water/atmosphere balances, instrument observations and uncertainty analysis.
Genuine30EC elective/minor space has no specified subject counterpart.
Required individual12EC Earth-system thesis has no taught-course equivalent. UCR’s optional15EC independent research is a separate opportunity outside the24-course/180EC schedule.

notes.text: WUR prescribes a deeper sequence in atmospheric physics and meteorology, hydrology, general chemistry, lowland sedimentology and coordinated field measurement, followed by an individual 12 EC thesis. The UCR programmes combine substantial Earth science, geochemistry, soils, water, ecology and geospatial or quantitative inquiry. They do not reproduce that full specialist sequence. UCR’s optional 15 EC independent research is additional to the illustrated 180 EC.

selection.assessment: Three sequentially tested responses materially engage the target: integrated Earth/environmental mechanisms and evidence; geospatial/computational environmental inquiry; and soil/water/biosphere resilience. All21eligible interests retain unique construction ownership. Quantitative, ecological and applied differences are substantive curricular choices and satisfy every pairwise30ECfloor. The scientific/fieldwork/thesis limitations remain explicit; no fourth programme is generated.

audience.programmeDescription: Earth System Sciences at Wageningen studies how soil, water, the atmosphere and the biosphere interact. English-taught scientific study combines physics, chemistry, mathematics, modelling and extensive practical work.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The first UCR programme combines Earth processes, climate, soils, water and environmental evidence. The second gives greater weight to geospatial and computational methods; the third to ecological mechanisms, land use and resilience. WUR adds its deeper atmospheric, hydrological and sedimentological sequence, coordinated field courses and required individual thesis.
